explanation: Fires on function words and name tokens inside software license and copyright header boilerplate (Apache/GPL/BSD/MIT text, 'Copyright (c) ... Ltd', 'This file is part of the Qt Toolkit'). The surrounding license-header context is what matters, not the particular token. The strongest single hit is on a broken byte in mojibake (garbled CJK) text. Outside license headers it is mostly silent.

Fires on CJK (Chinese/Japanese) word tokens, especially inside code: string resources, comments, placeholders like '请输入', and short UI labels. It also fires on Chinese/Japanese prose. Weaker, scattered hits on English tokens ('a ton', '-related', '-dependent') do not share an obvious theme.

Fires on words in contexts about places being open or closed to the public, or about attracting visitors, tourists, traffic or views: 'closed [to] traffic', 'opened [to] public', 'residents [and] visitors', 'attract', 'tourist', 'has [been] seen by'. Its strength depends on that access/visitor/traffic theme in the context. There are some looser web-server/traffic-forwarding hits ('redirect', 'forwards', '$remote_user').
Diffuse: fires on assorted mid-sentence tokens across very different genres (math word problems, scientific prose, code, biographies, licenses), with no clear shared token or context.

Fires on the token right after a verb or label that introduces a count, quantity or value: 'recorded [one] goal', 'contributing with [two] goals', 'thrown [an] NFL pass', 'GA [=]', '$input [=]', 'entered [into] regression'. It is strongest in sports-statistics and stats-methods contexts, plus assignment '=' in code. It is loosely coherent but noisy.

Fires strongly on the loop variable 'i' (or 't') right after 'for' / 'for (var' in code. It also fires on a mix of other things: the article 'a' after quantifiers ('quite a', 'ranged from a'), digits inside numbers, and letters inside acronyms. The loop-variable job is the clearest; the rest looks like a grab bag.

Fires on assorted tokens with no single theme. Several clusters stand out: academic degrees ('B.A.', 'undergraduate degree', 'licenciatura'), 'is' in 'The aim/purpose of this paper is', and section starts like 'Introduction' or 'Field of the Invention'. Others are unrelated (Random constructor, 'mammoth', 'chimpanzee').

Fires on website and license boilerplate phrasing: cookie notices ('personalised [service]', 'best [experience]'), terms-of-use and website instructions ('click', 'visit again', 'access'), and GPL/Apache stock lines ('if [not], write to', 'distributed [in] the hope'). The boilerplate context drives it, and the strongest hits come from cookie banners.

Two unrelated jobs. (1) It fires on the tag name right after '</' in HTML closing tags ('</[[a]]>', '</[[strong]]>', '</[[span]]>'). (2) It fires on tokens within discourse or hedging phrases in prose ('not a surprise [given]', 'difficult [to] delineate', 'needed [to] explore', 'To that [end]').
Diffuse: fires on varied tokens with no clear common thread, including score digits ('7-[[6]]', '10/1[[0]]'), 'as' in headlines, 'CANNOT', words in Q&A and error messages, and 'Prime [Minister]'.

Fires on a determiner or variable sigil at the start of a noun phrase that is the object of a verb or preposition: 'appeals from [a/an] order/decree', 'Apple Inc. and [the] Swift project', 'Version 2.0 ([the] "License")', 'increase [the] ...', and the '$' after '=' in PHP. It is mainly 'the/a' after a governing verb or preposition.

Fires on the token 'form' / 'Form' as a word or word piece in any language or sense: 'Form work', 'Formel', '-forming', 'formaldehyde', 'form' in HTML, 'Formatters', 'Formalism'. It is weaker for related words like 'formation' and 'morph'. The token identity is what matters.

Two jobs. (1) It fires on index or subscript variables in math or code ('a[[Xi]]-1', 'x^{[[n]]-1}', 'v[[[i]]]', 'Y_{[[n]]}'). (2) It fires on words in media republication and sharing boilerplate ('may not be published, broadcast, rewritten or [redistributed]', 'Email this [article]', 'Share this [post]').

Fires on the first token of a person's surname, or of a proper place name, that follows a first name or appears as the title of an entry ('Michael E. [Broadway]', 'Demarcus [Peoples]', '[Trou]sdale', 'William [Aber]hart'). It also fires on the first piece of species epithets. Starting a proper-name part is what matters.
Fires strongly on 'family' in taxonomic boilerplate ('is a moth of the [family] ...'). It also fires on assorted other tokens with no obvious link: 'The' in titles, inner word pieces, list items.

Fires near the start of a document, often on the first sentence boundary or on the first word of the next sentence or clause: '?', '.', 'And', 'While', 'It', 'Will', and words early in a title. Position early in the document seems to matter more than which token it is.

Fires on punctuation and identifier tokens in dense code syntax (C/C++/C#/JS/TS): closing quotes and brackets, ';', '();', ':' after object keys, template arguments, '_MSC_VER'. The code context drives it, and in prose it is almost silent.

Diffuse: fires on nouns ending a fixed phrase ('subject [matter]', 'this [list] of conditions', 'the [art]', 'the [Software]', 'guide [rail]') plus assorted code and config tokens. No clear single rule.

Fires on the token right after words like 'same', 'similar' or 'every' that set up a comparison or universal: 'in the same way [as]', 'example set [by]', 'as [with] all', 'similar mode [as]', 'same thing I do [with]', 'in [every] valve'. The comparison or 'same' framing in the preceding context drives it.

Fires on 'This' at the start of a sentence, strongest in file and code header comments ('* This file is part of', 'This code is distributed') and abstracts ('abstract: This paper'). It is weaker for sentence-initial 'this/These' in prose and for mid-sentence 'this'.

Fires on digit tokens in the middle or end of long numeric strings such as IDs, case and docket numbers, phone numbers, timestamps, DOIs/URLs and citation page numbers. It is strongest for long arbitrary digit sequences and weaker in years or times.
